questions.prompt: Which seeds may appear in a training log if the evaluation seeds are 1000-1099?
options: Only seeds below 1000, with a test for disjoint ranges.
Any seed at all, as long as the number of episodes is the same in both logs.
Seeds 1000-1099 as well, because evaluation and training episodes come from the same distribution.
Seeds above 1099, so evaluation is always later in time.
questions.explanation: Disjoint seed ranges, enforced by a test, are the cheapest protection against leakage.

questions.prompt: 18 successes in 20 episodes. Lower end of the 95 % Wilson interval (3 decimals).
questions.explanation: Wilson [0.699, 0.972]: with 20 episodes the interval is wide.

questions.prompt: 0 successes in 50 episodes. Upper end of the 95 % Wilson interval (3 decimals).
questions.explanation: Wilson [0.000, 0.071]: zero observed successes still allows about 7 %.

questions.prompt: Why is the Wilson interval preferred to the normal approximation for 29 successes in 30 episodes?
options: It is always narrower, which makes results look better.
It needs no assumption that episodes are independent.
The normal approximation can exceed 1 and is unreliable near 0 and 1.
It only works for 100 or more episodes.
questions.explanation: Wilson stays inside [0,1] and has better coverage for small n and extreme p. It still assumes independent episodes.

questions.prompt: Which setting list makes CPU PPO training repeatable on one machine?
options: A random seed for the environment only, since the policy network is deterministic anyway.
Larger vectorised environments, a fixed batch size and a fixed number of rollout steps.
A fixed wall-clock budget together with an automatic seed taken from the system time.
One torch thread, one numpy Generator, seeded python, torch and environment, pinned versions.
questions.explanation: Every source of randomness and every threaded reduction must be pinned.

questions.prompt: Two identical training runs differ in their logged evaluation return by 3e-3. Describe how you would find the cause.
rubric: Checks threads, seeding of every component and version differences first.
Logs the loss or parameters after every update in both runs and finds the first update that differs.
Fixes the cause and re-runs the reproducibility gate instead of loosening the tolerance.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: A BC policy trained on demos of joint-position targets is run with an end-effector-delta action space. Which test catches this before training?
options: Replay the demo actions open loop and check the scripted episode still succeeds.
Increase the number of demonstrations to 500 and retrain with a lower learning rate.
Compare the training loss with the validation loss after every single epoch.
Normalise the observations again with fresh statistics.
questions.explanation: A replay test needs no training and exposes any action-space or timing mismatch.

questions.prompt: Why must the BC train/validation split be made by demonstration rather than by timestep?
options: Timesteps are too few to split into two useful sets for an MLP.
Neighbouring timesteps are almost identical, so a timestep split leaks validation data.
Splitting by demonstration always makes the reported validation loss smaller.
The optimiser requires whole demonstrations in every mini-batch.
questions.explanation: Leakage between neighbouring frames makes validation MSE look better than it is.

questions.prompt: 8 environments give 500 steps per second in total. How many hours do 2 M steps take? (3 decimals)
Control runs at 20 Hz. An action delay of 120 ms must be simulated with a FIFO. How many whole control steps of buffering (round up)?
With discount gamma = 0.95, about how many steps is the effective horizon 1/(1-gamma)?
A reward pays +1 per step for being within 3 cm of the object and 10 once for lifting. What failure do you expect?
options: The policy will never move at all because the reward per step is much too small.
The policy will lift immediately because the bonus of 10 is large.
The policy may hover within 3 cm all episode, because that out-earns the lift.
The policy will leave the workspace to find more reward.
questions.explanation: A positive per-step pay for a pre-goal state can dominate a one-off goal bonus: reward hacking.

questions.prompt: Training uses mass 0.8-1.2, friction 0.7-1.3 and delay 0-30 ms. The held-out set is mass 0.7-1.3, friction 0.6-1.4, delay 40 ms. Propose new training ranges and say how you would report results.
rubric: Widens ranges so the held-out values are covered, in particular delay up to at least 50 ms.
Checks the scripted policy still succeeds at the extremes so the task stays feasible.
Reports nominal, in-range and out-of-range splits separately with Wilson intervals.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Five PPO seeds gave success counts 96, 61, 90, 88 and 20 out of 100. Write the paragraph of your report that describes this honestly.
rubric: Reports all five seeds and the mean (71 %) with an interval, not the best seed.
States that the learning gate fails and gives a hypothesis for the failing seed.
Proposes a follow-up experiment (more seeds or changed hyperparameters) fixed before evaluating.
